WasteWise

Know Before You Throw — an AI waste-sorting assistant for Yale SOM's Evans Hall, with an operations dashboard for the Sustainability Chair.

Rachel Rosenberg · Yale School of Management · 1Y Sustainability Chair
MGT 409: AI Foundations · Final Project · October 2026

Source code & setup https://github.com/rfr24/wastewise

How to run it: WasteWise is not publicly deployed, so there is no live URL. The working application runs locally — clone the repository above and follow the README.md: git clone → npm ci → npm start → http://localhost:3000. A fresh clone reached a working answer in seven seconds on a clean machine. npm test runs the full suite offline and needs no API key. The README also gives the one line needed to open the operations dashboard at /admin.

WasteWise answers "where does this go?" for a student standing at a waste station — from text or a photo — and refuses to answer beyond a curated, source-verified rule set. Every answer states how well confirmed it is.

2

Motivation

Evans Hall has waste stations on every floor, and the signage on them is not consistent. Some stations carry detailed labels; some carry almost none. A student finishing lunch between classes has a coffee cup, a wrapper, and thirty seconds.

This project began from informal conversations with my Yale SOM classmates, in the ordinary course of my role as 1Y Sustainability Chair — hallway and lunch-table conversations, not a survey or a study. Three themes came up repeatedly, and I am paraphrasing the substance rather than quoting anyone:

  • Coffee cups. People assume a paper cup is recyclable because it is paper. Classmates were surprised to learn Yale excludes them, and surprised again that the lid and sleeve may be handled differently from the cup.
  • Compostable packaging. Items printed with "compostable" were assumed to belong in a compost or food-waste bin — the label was read as naming the bin. It does not. Yale's published guidance is explicit that compostable utensils, plates and cups are neither recyclable nor accepted in food-waste bins, and should go in the trash. Beyond those named items, acceptance depends on the material and on what the local collection programme actually takes, and what Evans Hall collects is not something I have been able to confirm.
  • "Recycling it is the safer guess." Several classmates worked from the belief that when you are unsure, putting an item in recycling is the conservative choice. It is the opposite: the wrong item can contaminate a whole load, which is why the app refuses to guess rather than guessing optimistically.

The cost here is not dramatic, and I want to be careful not to overstate it. It is measured in seconds of hesitation many times a day, in confident wrong guesses, and in the gap between people wanting to sort correctly and having no reliable way to check. Existing resources are not organized around the moment of decision: Yale's recycling guidance is a set of web pages, read in advance or not at all.

What this project does not claim. Friends have tried WasteWise informally, but it has had no structured testing with students and no formal evaluation, and it does not measure contamination rates, diversion rates, or behaviour change. The conversations above are qualitative motivation for building it, not evidence that it works. Section 7 is explicit about what evidence exists and what does not.
3

What is new here

Waste sorting help already exists. The honest question is what WasteWise does that these do not.

Existing solutionWhat it doesGap for an Evans Hall student
Yale Recycling website and FAQ Authoritative Yale-wide guidance on accepted materials, published as web pages. Correct but not situational. You must know which page answers your item, and it does not address a specific building.
RecycleCT "In the Bin" Statewide Connecticut search tool for whether an item is accepted. Statewide rules, not Yale's. Yale defers to it for items it does not name, which a student would have no way to know.
How2Recycle labels Standardized on-package labels from the Sustainable Packaging Coalition telling you how to recycle that packaging. Only on member brands' packaging, and describes general recyclability — not whether this building collects it.
Recycle Coach Municipal sorting app with a "What Goes Where" search; adopted by some campuses, including UC Santa Cruz. Keyed to a municipality or participating campus. Yale SOM is not a participant, and it does not model building-level uncertainty.
Campus sorting guides (e.g. Waterloo Shift:Zero, CWRU's QR-code bin signs) Campus-specific searchable sorting guides, some reached by QR codes at bins. Closest comparison, and good practice. They work as lookup tools — you ask about an item you can name — and the published versions surface no view of what students are collectively asking.
General-purpose ChatGPT Will answer any sorting question immediately, including from a photo. Answers from general knowledge, typically with an even tone whether or not the ground is firm. It has no access to Evans Hall's signage, and nothing ties its confidence to a citable local source.

Three things WasteWise does differently

1. It is retrieval-grounded and refuses to exceed its sources. The model is never asked what it knows about recycling. Each question retrieves matching rules from a curated knowledge base, and only those rules go into the prompt. A deterministic code guardrail then re-checks the model's stated confidence against the verification status of the rules it actually cited, and downgrades it when the model overstates. The model cannot leak Yale policy it was never given.

2. Verification status is a first-class concept, not a disclaimer. Every rule is verified (cited to a published Yale or Connecticut source), observational (photographed Evans Hall signage — reported as an observation, never as confirmed policy), or unverified (no source found; the app says so). Where a Yale-wide rule and local signage conflict, both are recorded and the conflict is surfaced rather than resolved by guessing.

3. It is instrumented for the person who can fix the signage. This is the part no comparison above does. The operations dashboard turns the questions students ask into a standing view of where the building's guidance is unclear — which is exactly the input a Sustainability Chair needs for Facilities conversations (Section 7).

4

The agents

Two model passes with deliberately unequal knowledge, plus deterministic code between and after them.

Architecture

AgentRoleModelSees the rules?
Vision pass Returns a structured array of the distinct objects visible (max 8), each with material, form, condition, visible text, and explicit uncertainty flags. Its prompt forbids naming a bin. gpt-6-luna No — a test asserts vision.js cannot even import the rules module
Reasoning pass One call covering every item. Each item gets its own retrieval and its own guardrail pass, so a scone and its wrapper get different answers. gpt-6-luna Only the rules retrieved for that item

Why this model. gpt-6-luna is the course-provided model via the Portkey gateway. Before any photo UI was built, I verified that image input actually worked on it by sending a generated red-circle PNG and confirming the model returned {"shape":"circle","color":"red"}. Vision support was tested, not assumed.

Why two passes with unequal knowledge. If one call both identified the object and chose the bin, the model's general knowledge about recycling would leak into the decision and there would be no way to tell grounded answers from recalled ones. Splitting them means the identification step is a perception task and the routing step is a retrieval task, and the retrieval step can be audited.

One real run, traced end to end

Question: "I have a clear plastic clamshell container from a salad, is that recyclable in Evans Hall?" — the same question that exposed three real defects during development, all fixed and regression-tested.

  1. Input screening

    Text is length-capped at 500 characters, stripped of control characters, and screened for injection patterns before anything else runs. This question passes clean and is wrapped in <question> tags, designating it as data rather than instruction.

  2. Rule retrieval

    Alias matching with word boundaries over 24 rules returns exactly one: rigid-plastic-container (verified). Getting there took two fixes.

    Defect 1 — an incidental word drove the match. The food rule carries the alias "salad", so "container from a salad" scored a specific match on food scraps and dragged in the Evans Hall compost rules with it. That word describes what the container held, not the object being thrown away. The fix ignores a food word when it sits in a container shape — "salad container", "container from a salad" — while leaving "half-eaten sandwich in a plastic container" alone, because that one really is food.

    Defect 2 — a genuine knowledge gap. Nothing covered a rigid plastic container at all, so the app could only say it did not know. The sources did support an answer: Yale single-stream accepts plastics #1, #2 and #5 and requires them clean and empty, and RecycleCT — the statewide list Yale's own FAQ directs people to for items Yale does not name — lists "Plastic containers, tubs & lids" as accepted. That became one new verified rule.

  3. Fast path declines, deliberately

    The rule is marked conditional, which makes it ineligible for the zero-token fast path. The stream depends on the resin number, so the shortcut must never fire a bare "recycling" with the conditions stripped off. The question goes to the model.

  4. Reasoning pass

    One API call. The prompt contains the system instructions and only the retrieved rules. Measured: 2,758 input tokens (2,755 written to cache), 1,089 output tokens of which 933 were reasoning tokens. End-to-end 10.7 s.

  5. Guardrails re-check the answer in code

    enforceVerification() compares the model's stated confidence against the actual verification status of the rules it cited, and downgrades it if overstated. Hazard screening runs independently. Unsupported "otherwise put it in the trash" fallbacks are stripped.

  6. The app gives a conditional recycling recommendation

    The recorded outcome is recommendation: recycling, confidence: confirmed, with no follow-up question:

    "Recycle it if it's stamped #1, #2, or #5 and is empty and wiped clean; otherwise, including if it has no number, put it in the trash."

    Defect 3 — the prompt overrode the rule. Getting that sentence took one more fix. The system prompt listed "what resin number is stamped on a plastic item" as a must-ask case, so the model kept returning an empty answer and a question instead. That clause now reads: if a verified rule states the outcome for every value the missing fact could take, give both branches rather than asking. A question is only worth asking when you cannot hand the student a complete answer without it. The response above was identical across three consecutive runs.

    On the trash branch. Yale publishes which plastics are accepted, not a list of what is refused, and it does not name clamshells. The trash half therefore follows by exclusion — an item not on the accepted list must not go into the recycling stream — which is how the existing verified cold-cup rule is worded too. Nothing here claims Yale names this item, and the rule text says so explicitly.

    The loop that produced this. The knowledge gap was not found by reading code. The dashboard surfaced it as "Add a sourced rule for Rigid plastic takeout container", with the evidence that it had been asked four times and ended without a recommendation every time (Figure 6). That is the mechanism described in Section 7, working on its own author.

  7. Answer and log

    The student sees one short instruction, a confidence label, and an expandable "Rules used" list with the Yale citations. The row is logged with tokens, outcome, latency and cohort. No account, user id, session id or IP address is attached to the row, and the photo is never written anywhere. The cohort is a group label, not a per-person identifier. The question text is the one caveat: it is stored verbatim and is free-form.

Tokenomics

Every API call records exact input, cached input, and output token counts. The figures below come from 22 real runs that carry full cache accounting, not from estimates.

Measured tokens per run

RunInputCached input Output(of which reasoning)Cost
Text question, cold cache (id 89)2,7580 1,089933$0.000820
Identical question, warm cache (id 90)2,7582,755 1,064860$0.000560
Fast-path question (no API call)00 00$0.000000
Mean of all 22 measured AI runs2,716 1,501624 395$0.000448

Across those 22 runs the median cost was $0.000377 and the range $0.000182–$0.001624; the most expensive was a multi-item photo. Reasoning tokens were about 63% of all output, which is why output dominates cost on this model.

Pricing basis — read this before using any dollar figure

Costs use OpenAI's published list prices for gpt-6-luna (pricing page, retrieved 16 October 2026): $0.10 per 1M input tokens, $0.01 per 1M cached input tokens, $0.50 per 1M output tokens.

This app reaches the model through the course's Portkey gateway. These are therefore list-price estimates applied to exact measured token counts — not a record of money actually billed to anyone. Cached tokens are a subset of input tokens and reasoning tokens are a subset of output tokens; both are billed once, at the correct rate, never added on top.

Prompt caching is real on this model, and it was verified

I did not assume caching existed. Two identical calls were sent and the usage objects compared: the first reported cache_write_tokens: 2755 and cached_tokens: 0; the second reported the reverse. 99.9% of the prompt was served from cache on the repeat. That is what makes the warm run 32% cheaper than the cold one.

Across all 22 measured runs, 55% of every input token billed was served from cache, and 16 of the 22 hit a warm cache. The app's system prompt and rules block are substantially identical between questions, which is exactly the shape caching rewards.

It also changes how cost must be calculated. Charging cached tokens at the full input rate would have overstated the warm run by about a third. The cost function splits them.

Cost at scale

Taking the mean across all 22 measured runs — $0.000448 per model-answered question — and assuming four questions per user per month:

ScaleQuestions/monthMonthly cost Annual cost
All development testing to date22 measured runs $0.0099 total—
100 users400$0.18$2.15
10,000 users40,000$17.94$215

Model inference is not the constraint on this project at any realistic campus scale. The entire SOM student body asking four questions each per month would cost well under a dollar. Every development run so far — 22 measured AI calls — has cost about one cent in total.

Why the dashboard shows a smaller cost figure than this section

The Overview tab reports cost as known for only a minority of recorded questions, and shows that subset totalling $0.00. Both statements are correct, and they are measuring different things:

  • The per-run figures above are the 22 runs that carry full token and cache accounting, priced from their exact counts. They describe what one model-answered question costs.
  • The dashboard total covers historical development queries. Most were recorded before per-token rates were configured, so their cost is stored as null — unknown, not zero — and the dashboard reports that as partial coverage rather than summing to a confident total.
  • Many of the rows it can price are fast-path answers, which made no API call and genuinely cost $0.00. A real zero, not a missing value — which is why the dashboard's priced subset sums to so little.

No historical row was back-priced to make the dashboard agree with this section. Retroactively applying today's rates to old queries would produce a tidier number and a false one.

Cost-cutting steps, and what they traded away

StepMeasured effectTrade-off
Deterministic fast path. Unambiguous, verified, non-generic text questions are answered from the rule set with no API call. 16 recorded questions cost zero tokens and $0.00, answered in 0–6 ms (seven measured fast-path answers) instead of seconds. Real and serious. An early version matched the bare word "paper" and answered "paper plate" as recycling. Fixing it required marking generic and conditional rules ineligible — which narrowed the fast path. Correctness won; see Section 6.
Prompt caching on the repeated system prompt and rules block. 2,755 of 2,758 input tokens served from cache on a repeat; warm run 32% cheaper. None observed. The cache is managed upstream.
Client-side image downscale to 1600px before upload. Roughly 12× smaller uploads, cutting both transfer time and vision input tokens. Fine detail is lost. Small printed resin codes can become unreadable — which is partly why the app asks rather than guessing when a code is not legible.
One reasoning call per photo, however many items are in it. A four-item photo costs two calls total, not five. A single malformed response affects all items, so the parser degrades a missing item to unknown rather than letting it inherit a neighbour's bin.

Totals at the time Figure 4 was captured: 98 recorded questions, 412,844 input tokens and 108,499 output tokens. Almost all of that is development iteration over nine days of building, not representative student usage.

6

Safety

Three risks matter for this app: giving confidently wrong disposal advice, being manipulated through its inputs, and spending money without limit.

Risk 1 — Confidently wrong advice

This is the real risk. A wrong answer delivered confidently is worse than no app, because it converts a student's uncertainty into misplaced trust, and because the wrong item in a recycling stream can contaminate a load.

Defence: a deterministic guardrail that outranks the model. enforceVerification() runs in code after every response. It re-reads the verification status of the rules the model actually cited and downgrades any confidence the sources do not support. A model answer of "confirmed" grounded only in observational signage cannot survive it.

Defence: hazards are over-blocked on purpose. A potentially hazardous item — battery, electronics, chemical, sharp, medication, bulb, aerosol — never receives a station bin, even when the model answers confidently. The guardrail overrides the recommendation and routes to Yale EHS. The check is deliberately over-inclusive: a false positive sends someone to EHS unnecessarily, while a false negative could put a lithium battery in a bin.

A defence that caught a real failure

During development the rule for clean paper carried a bare alias, "paper". A student asking about a paper plate matched it, and because the match looked unambiguous and verified, the zero-token fast path answered "recycling — confirmed". That is exactly the failure mode this project exists to prevent, and it shipped past earlier tests.

The fix was structural rather than a prompt tweak: dedicated paper-plate and paper-towel rules, bare material words scored as non-specific, and a generic flag that makes a rule ineligible for the fast path entirely. A regression test now asserts that generic material words cannot carry a match on their own, and that the fast path refuses ambiguous packaging.

Risk 2 — Prompt injection and hostile input

  • User text is wrapped in <question> tags and designated as data by the system prompt. Recognised injection patterns are flagged and surfaced in the response as flagged_input.
  • The vision prompt treats text visible inside a photo as data to report, never as instructions to follow — the obvious attack for a camera-driven app.
  • Uploads are restricted to JPEG, PNG and WebP, capped at 5 MB, and the declared media type is checked against the file's actual magic bytes. A script renamed to .jpg is rejected before reaching the API.
  • The deepest defence is architectural: the model holds no Yale policy knowledge to leak, because it is only ever given the rules retrieved for the current question.

Risk 3 — Runaway cost and abuse

  • Per-IP sliding-window rate limit (10 questions/minute by default), with a separate, roomier budget for feedback, which makes no API call.
  • A hard daily cap on billable calls (300 by default) so a loop or bot cannot run up the bill.
  • 500-character limit on questions, bounding input tokens.

Risk 4 — Exposure of the dashboard and credentials

The operations dashboard is admin-only: one shared secret, held server-side, exchanged for an HMAC-signed HttpOnly session cookie, compared in constant time. If no password is configured the admin area stays switched off rather than falling open. Admin sign-in over plaintext HTTP is refused outright in production. Diagnostics cannot be enabled in production whatever the environment says. No API key ever reaches the browser, and the repository has been scanned and verified to contain no secrets, no database, and no private photos.

Evidence these defences work

335 automated tests pass across 16 files, offline and deterministic — no test calls the model API. They include direct assertions that hazard and conflict protections hold, that generic material words cannot carry a match, that the fast path refuses ambiguous packaging, that an unverified rule can never answer "confirmed", that vision.js cannot import the rules module, and that every rule marked verified cites a real *.yale.edu URL.

7

Impact

Stating the evidence plainly. WasteWise has not yet been used by students and has not been formally evaluated. Friends have tried it informally and given feedback that shaped the wording and the photo flow, but that is not a study: there were no tasks, no measurements, and no record of who used it — informal use lands in the same development cohort as my own testing and is not separable from it afterwards. The recorded questions are development traffic, almost all of it mine. No change in sorting behaviour, contamination or diversion has been measured, and this report claims none. What follows is the mechanism by which the project could produce value — not a measured result.

What is demonstrated, and what is potential

ClaimStatusEvidence
Students are confused about coffee cups, "compostable" packaging, and contamination Demonstrated qualitatively Informal conversations with SOM classmates in my Sustainability Chair role. Paraphrased, not quoted; not a survey.
The assistant answers these questions from cited sources, and declines when it cannot Demonstrated Working app, 335 passing tests, the traced run in Section 4.
Questions can be turned into specific, actionable signage tasks Demonstrated mechanically Dashboard generates four opportunities end to end (Figure 6) — on development traffic, and it caught a real gap in the app itself.
The app is usable by someone other than its author Demonstrated informally Friends have tried it and given feedback, which changed the answer wording and the photo flow. Not a study — no tasks, no measurements, no participant record.
Students sort more accurately after using it Not demonstrated No formal evaluation has occurred. No measurement exists.
Contamination or diversion rates improve Not demonstrated The app does not measure either, and makes no such claim.
Facilities acts on the dashboard Potential A plan for my role. Facilities has not seen or adopted the tool.

The three confusions set out in Section 2 — paraphrased from informal conversations, never quoted — are the qualitative basis for all of this. They are observations about confusion, which is precisely what WasteWise is built to answer and to record.

The mechanism: a feedback loop into Facilities conversations

The durable value of this project is not the answer given to one student. It is that the questions students ask are themselves the data a Sustainability Chair has never had.

Yale SOM Facilities is the building operations team responsible for managing or coordinating waste collection and bin infrastructure in Evans Hall; their exact remit is one of the things I intend to confirm. As 1Y Sustainability Chair I meet with them biweekly. Those conversations are currently driven by impressions. WasteWise's dashboard is designed to replace impressions with a standing, anonymous record of what the building's occupants are actually confused about:

  • Recurring questions identify where signage is failing. If the same item is asked about repeatedly on one floor, that is a specific, actionable signage request rather than a general complaint.
  • Unresolved answers show where guidance genuinely does not exist. The app recording that it could not answer is useful information.
  • Thumbs-down feedback flags answers that were correct but unhelpful — a wording or education problem rather than a rules problem.
  • Consolidated opportunities convert the above into concrete next steps, each shown with its supporting evidence rather than as a bare assertion.

Running against development data, the dashboard surfaced the four opportunities in Figure 6, which illustrate the different kinds of action it distinguishes:

Opportunity surfacedKindWhat it would prompt
Verify food-scrap collection at Evans HallOpen question A direct question for Facilities — the single most valuable thing this project could resolve.
Add a sourced rule for "Rigid plastic takeout container"Knowledge gap A gap in the knowledge base, fixable without Facilities — and already acted on. It was asked four times and never answered; checking Yale and RecycleCT produced the verified rule traced in Section 4.
Signpost the deciding detail for "Batteries"Signage opportunity Asked three times, two needing a clarification first. One detail decides it and is not apparent at the bin — a concrete signage suggestion.
Review how WasteWise answers about "Paper towel, napkin, or tissue" Unhelpful feedback A wording problem flagged by a thumbs-down, not a rules problem.

These are generated from development traffic and are shown to demonstrate that the mechanism works end to end. They are not findings about student behaviour. The dashboard says so itself, in two banners visible in Figure 6: that the view mixes development testing with any real usage, and that 50 early multi-item photos are excluded from the patterns.

Facilities has not seen this tool yet. No part of this project has been presented to or endorsed by SOM Facilities or Yale Recycling. I intend to bring it to our first biweekly meeting after fall break. The feedback loop described above is a plan I will pursue in my role, not an arrangement that exists.

What would make this measurable

A structured evaluation with recruited students is the next step, and the app is already built for it: a /eval link tags those sessions as student_eval via a signed cookie, keeping them separate from both my development testing and organic use, so the first real data is not contaminated by the development rows already in the database.

8

Limits and next steps

Limits

LimitDetail
No structured student testing yet Friends have used it informally and given feedback, but with no tasks, no measurements and no record of who used it. The recorded questions are development traffic from nine days of building, almost all of it mine. Nothing here measures student behaviour.
Evans Hall compost is unconfirmed Yale states it lacks capacity for compost service in non-dining spaces but does not name Evans Hall. Three rules remain unverified pending confirmation with SOM building operations, and the app will not tell a student their scraps are composted.
Signage rules are observations Four rules come from photographed Evans Hall signage. They can never answer "confirmed", and where they conflict with Yale-wide guidance the app surfaces the conflict rather than resolving it.
Response time is slow for model-answered questions Measured 10.7 s and 9.1 s on the two traced runs, driven largely by reasoning tokens. Fast-path answers returned in 0–6 ms across the seven that carry a recorded measurement. All of these are small samples describing specific runs, not a general performance claim. Latency is only recorded from the release that added the field, so dashboard coverage is partial and says so.
Partial analytics coverage 50 early multi-item photos predate per-item records and can never be itemised. The dashboard reports this as a coverage gap rather than hiding it.
Cost figures are list-price estimates Exact token counts, published list prices, no observed invoice.
Single process Rate limits and the daily cap live in process memory and reset on restart. SQLite is single-writer. Fine for one building; would need work to scale.
Model output varies between runs The deterministic guardrails constrain what can be said, not which phrasing comes back.
Not an official Yale service A student project. It does not speak for Yale Recycling, EHS, or SOM Facilities.

Next steps, in order

Committed

  1. Bring WasteWise to the first biweekly Facilities meeting after fall break. I already meet with the SOM Facilities team on that cadence as 1Y Sustainability Chair. The agenda is to demonstrate the prototype and talk through the sorting problems the dashboard has surfaced.
  2. Confirm what Evans Hall actually collects. The highest-value action available, and it requires no code. A written answer would promote three unverified rules and resolve the dashboard's top open question.
  3. Identify signage and guidance opportunities from the same conversation — the dashboard already names candidates, such as signposting the deciding detail for batteries.

Proposed, and contingent on that conversation

  1. Explore school funding for low-cost public hosting. If Facilities is receptive, I would ask whether SOM would fund hosting. I have researched the options and approximate costs — roughly $7/month for a managed host with a persistent volume. No funding has been requested, offered or granted, and nothing is deployed.
  2. Run a small QR-code pilot at a few Evans Hall stations, with sessions tagged through the existing /eval cohort so the first real usage data stays cleanly separated from my development testing.
  3. Feed what students ask back into Facilities conversations, which is the premise of Section 7 and the only way to test whether it holds.
  4. Expand the knowledge base as questions reveal gaps, keeping the same rule: no rule enters as verified without a citation.

In closing

WasteWise exists because a student at a bin has thirty seconds and no reliable way to check. The technical contribution is not that a model can answer the question — it is the architecture that stops it answering beyond what can be cited: retrieval over a curated, source-verified rule set, a deterministic guardrail that outranks the model, and a verification status attached to every answer. That design is what let the app say "I can't confirm this" instead of guessing, and what turned one unanswered question into a sourced rule during this project's own development.

What it does not yet have is students. The next step is the one that needs no code: taking the dashboard to my first biweekly Facilities meeting after fall break and confirming what Evans Hall actually collects.

WasteWise is built with Node 24 and Express, SQLite via the built-in node:sqlite module, and no frontend build step. The repository is public at github.com/rfr24/wastewise and runs from a fresh clone in under ten seconds following the README. The token, cost and latency measurements were taken on 16 October 2026; the dashboard screenshots and the traced run shown here are from 25 October 2026, after the sorting fixes described in Section 4. All of them can be reproduced from the repository.
